title: The 8 building blocks of AWX
preflight: Lab VM running (snapshot AWX installed). Open http://192.168.100.102:30080 and log in as admin; the password was changed in episode 2

SSH password login works on the VM: grep -i '^PasswordAuthentication' /etc/ssh/sshd_config must not say no, and systemctl is-active sshd says active. The ansible user does NOT exist yet on either node: you create it on camera (delete it first with userdel -r ansible if it is left from a test)
AWX pods all Running: k3s kubectl -n awx get pods
Browser at 100 percent zoom, dark theme, one clean tab, bookmarks bar hidden
Remove any old objects from episode tests (Homelab org, lab-ssh, series-repo, lab, ping-lab) so you build them live
Do NOT show the admin password or the ansible user's password on screen (pause recording with P while typing them)
Host PC has about 3 GB RAM and 10+ GB disk free for the second VM (node2 is a full clone of the lab VM)
Remove node2 from earlier tests (VirtualBox: Remove > Delete all files) so you build it live

steps.title: Open
steps.show: AWX dashboard in the browser, logged in as admin. Left menu visible.
steps.say: In episode two we installed AWX. Now you log in and see a wall of menus. Today I map every screen to one of eight objects: organization, credential, project, inventory, job template, workflow, schedule and execution environment. We build all eight on the lab VM, and you run a real job.

steps.title: Prep 1. Clone the VM to make a second node
steps.show: VirtualBox: shut down the lab VM. Right-click it > Clone. Name awx-node2, MAC address policy 'Generate new MAC addresses for all network adapters', Full clone, Current machine state. Then Settings on awx-node2: 1 vCPU, 2048 MB RAM. Start it and log in on the console as root. Run the commands one by one. Check node2 shows 192.168.100.103, then start the lab VM again.
cmd: nmcli con mod "<host-only connection name>" ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.168.100.103/24
steps.say: Before we touch the AWX screens, we prepare the lab. AWX runs on this VM, so we need a second machine for it to manage. In VirtualBox I shut the VM down, right click, Clone. A full clone makes an independent copy of the disk. I tick generate new MAC addresses, so the two machines do not collide on the network. Now the copy needs its own identity. Set hostname gives it the name node two. Removing the machine ID and running systemd machine id setup creates a fresh one, because two machines should never share it. Deleting the SSH host keys and running ssh keygen minus A creates new ones, so each machine has its own fingerprint. Next, systemctl disable now k3s plus the killall script stop Kubernetes. This node does not run AWX, it is only a target. Finally the network. IP dash br a shows the address, which is still the copy of node one. N M C L I connection show lists the connection name. Then connection modify sets a manual address, one nought three, and connection up applies it. One more IP dash br a to confirm it now says one nought three.
steps.watch: Pause (P) if the clone takes long. Use the real connection name from 'nmcli con show --active' (the one holding 192.168.100.x). Final ip -br a must show 192.168.100.103/24.

steps.title: Prep 2. Create the ansible user on node2
steps.show: Terminal on node2 (VirtualBox console, or ssh root@192.168.100.103), as root. Run the commands one by one. Type the password off camera (press P to pause) when passwd asks.
steps.say: Second prep step: an account for AWX to log in with, on node two. Never use root for this, a dedicated user is safer and easier to audit. User add creates the ansible user with a home folder and a bash shell. Passwd sets its password. Then we write one line into a sudoers file: ansible may run all commands, with no password prompt, because automation cannot type one. Chmod four four zero locks the file down, sudo requires that. Visudo minus c f checks the syntax, so a typo cannot lock us out. The last command logs in as ansible and runs sudo whoami. It prints root, which proves the account works. Node one only runs AWX, so it does not need this user. We use the account in the credential and the inventory in a moment.
steps.watch: Last command must print: root. Pause recording while typing the password.

steps.title: The eight objects on the menu
steps.show: Expand the left menu: Resources, Access, Administration. Hover each item without clicking.
steps.say: Almost every menu item is one of eight objects. Access holds organizations, users and teams. Resources holds templates, credentials, projects and inventories. Administration holds execution environments, notifications and settings. Hold that picture, we build them in this order, because each one needs the one before it.

steps.title: 1. Organization
steps.show: Access > Organizations. Show Default. Add: name Homelab, description Series lab. Save.
steps.say: One: the organization. It is the top level container. Everything below belongs to an organization, and permissions are handed out per organization. We keep Default untouched and create Homelab.

steps.title: 2. Credential
steps.show: AWX: Resources > Credentials > Add. Name lab-ssh, organization Homelab, credential type Machine, username ansible (the user from Prep 2), password (type it off camera, press P). Privilege escalation method sudo, privilege escalation username root, leave its password empty. Save. Point at the lock icon: the password shows as Encrypted.
steps.say: Two: the credential. It holds the login AWX uses on your machines. Resources, Credentials, Add. The name is lab-ssh, in the Homelab organization. The type is Machine, which means a login for a server. Username is ansible, the user from the prep, and the password goes here. Privilege escalation method sudo lets playbooks become root when they need to. Save, and look: the password now says Encrypted. AWX never shows it again, and people who can use the credential cannot read it.
steps.watch: Do not show the password. Pause recording while you type it, then resume.

steps.title: 3a. Show the Git repo
steps.show: Browser tab on GitHub: github.com/Venuvgp19/Youtube-Tutorials-Awx. Open the ep03 folder and ping.yml. Then click the green Code button and copy the HTTPS URL.
steps.say: Before the project, look at where it comes from. AWX never edits playbooks itself. They live in Git. This is our series repo, and here is the playbook we will run, ep zero three slash ping dot yml. Click Code, copy the HTTPS address. That is all AWX needs. The repo is public, so no password is needed. For a private repo you add a source control credential, and we do that in episode five.
steps.watch: Zoom on the copied URL ending in .git.

steps.title: 3b. Connect the repo to AWX (Project)
steps.show: AWX: Resources > Projects > Add. Name series-repo, organization Homelab, source control type Git, paste the URL, branch main. Leave 'Update revision on job launch' ticked. Save. Wait for the green Successful status, then open the project Jobs tab and show the sync job output.
steps.say: Three: the project. This is where you connect the repo to AWX. Name it, pick Git as the source control type, paste the address and set the branch to main. I also tick update revision on job launch, so every job runs the latest playbook. Save, and AWX clones the repo. Green Successful means AWX now sees every playbook in it. Open the sync job to see the git clone happen.
steps.watch: Show the sync job output once. Press Speed during the wait if it takes long. If it fails, check internet from the VM (NIC 2 NAT).

steps.title: 4. Inventory
steps.show: Resources > Inventories > Add > Add inventory. Name lab, organization Homelab. Save. Then Hosts > Add: name 192.168.100.103 (node2 from the prep). Save.
steps.say: Four: the inventory. It is the list of machines a job can touch. Here it is one host, node two, the machine we cloned in the prep. AWX itself stays on node one. Later episodes use groups, variables and dynamic sources like AWS.
steps.watch: Host must be 192.168.100.103, not the AWX node.

steps.title: 5. Execution environment
steps.show: Administration > Execution Environments. Open AWX EE (latest) and show the image name. Do not change anything.
steps.say: Five: the execution environment. A job does not run on the AWX web pod. It runs inside a container image that carries Ansible and its collections. That image is the execution environment. We use the default one now, and in episode seven we build our own.

steps.title: 6. Job template
steps.show: Resources > Templates > Add > Add job template. Name ping-lab, job type Run, inventory lab, project series-repo, execution environment default, playbook ep03/ping.yml, credential lab-ssh, and tick Privilege escalation. Save, then Launch.
steps.say: Six: the job template, and this is where it comes together. A job template is a recipe: this playbook, from this project, on this inventory, with this credential, in this execution environment. Tick privilege escalation so the playbook can use sudo. Launch it, and watch the output stream live. The last task prints root, which proves the ansible user has full access on node two.
steps.watch: Wait for Successful. If unreachable, test from node1: ssh ansible@192.168.100.103. See the README troubleshooting table.

steps.title: 7. Workflow template
steps.show: Resources > Templates > Add > Add workflow template. Name sync-then-ping, organization Homelab. Save, then Visualizer > Start > Add node: Project Sync series-repo. Add a second node on success: Job template ping-lab. Save and Launch.
steps.say: Seven: the workflow. A workflow chains templates and projects into a flow, with branches for success and failure. Here it syncs the repo first, then runs the ping. Episode nine goes deep on approvals and failure paths.

steps.title: 8. Schedule
steps.show: Open job template ping-lab > Schedules > Add. Name every-5-min, start now, frequency Minute, every 5. Save and point at the Next run time. Then turn the toggle off.
steps.say: Eight: the schedule. Any template can run on a timer. Pick a start time and a frequency, and AWX launches it for you. I turn it off now, so it does not spam the lab.
steps.watch: Turn the schedule off before moving on, or it keeps launching jobs.

steps.title: The whole picture
steps.show: Open the job template ping-lab details and point at each field in turn: inventory, project, execution environment, credential. Then the Organizations list.
steps.say: That is the whole map. A job template points to a project, an inventory, a credential and an execution environment, and all of them live inside an organization. A workflow chains templates. A schedule triggers them. If you can name these eight, you can read any AWX screen.

steps.title: Close
steps.say: Next time: your first job from scratch, from a Git project to a job template you launch yourself. All the commands are in the repo, in the ep zero three folder. Thanks for watching, and see you in the next one.
